question.md:
Slide a window of `k` consecutive readings from the start to the end, one hour at a time. For each of the
`n − k + 1` positions, report the highest reading in view.

- **Readings can repeat and be negative.**
- **`k` can be 1** (every reading is its own peak) or `n` (a single window).
- **Up to 10⁵ readings and `k` up to `n`**, so `n × k` can reach 10¹⁰.

think.md:
Readings `[3, 1, -2, 5, 4, 2, 0, 6]` with `k = 3`. The windows' peaks are `[3, 5, 5, 5, 4, 6]`.

When the 5 arrives at hour 3, the readings 1 and −2 before it are still in view for a while, but they'll never
be the peak again: the 5 is higher and will stay on screen longer than they will. So they can be forgotten.
What's left is always a **decreasing** list of candidates: each one is the peak of the future windows until
something higher arrives or it scrolls off.

think.caption: Once 5 is in view, 1 and −2 can never be a peak again.

think.md:
New candidates join at the back (after removing the weaker ones there), and expired ones leave from the front:
a double-ended queue. The front is the oldest surviving candidate and the highest, so it's the peak.

approaches.title: Scan every window

idea.md: For each window start `i`, scan `temps[i..i+k−1]` for the maximum.

build: For `i` from 0 to `n − k`: compute the max of the window.

lines.text: One peak per window: `n − k + 1` of them.
Highest of the `k` readings in view.

complexity.md: **Time O(n·k):** up to 10¹⁰ for large windows. **Space O(1)** beyond the answer.

walk.title: Look at every window and scan all k readings for the highest.

limits.md: Neighbouring windows share `k − 1` readings, and the scan redoes all of them. Either precompute block maxima, or keep only the readings that can still be a peak.

approaches.title: Block running maxima

idea.md: Split the array into blocks of `k`. Compute `fromStart[i]` (max from `i`'s block start to `i`) and `toEnd[i]` (max from `i` to its block's end). A window `i..i+k−1` is the tail of one block plus the head of the next (or exactly one block), so its peak is `max(toEnd[i], fromStart[i+k−1])`.

build: Forward pass: `fromStart[i]` restarts at each block boundary (`i % k == 0`).
Backward pass: `toEnd[i]` restarts at each block's last index (or the array end).
Each window's peak is the max of the two lookups.

lines.text: Two copies of the readings to turn into running maxima.
Running max from the start of each block; it restarts when `i` is a multiple of `k`.
Running max back from the end of each block; it restarts at each block's last index.
Window `i..i+k−1` = (tail of `i`'s block) + (head of the next block up to `i+k−1`). If `i` starts a block, both lookups cover the same whole block. Either way, the peak is the larger lookup.

complexity.md: **Time O(n):** two passes plus one lookup per window. **Space O(n)** for the two arrays.

walk.title: Cut the readings into blocks of k = 3. Any window covers the end of one block and the start of the next, so its peak = max(best from i to its block's end, best from the next block's start to the window's end).

limits.md: Linear, but it needs the whole array up front and two extra arrays of size n. The deque handles readings as they stream in, using only O(k) memory.

approaches.title: Monotonic deque

idea.md: Keep a deque of indices whose readings strictly decrease front to back. For each hour `i`: pop from the back while the back's reading ≤ `temps[i]`; push `i`; if the front index is `≤ i − k`, it has scrolled off, so pop it from the front. Once `i ≥ k − 1`, the front is the peak.

build: For each hour: clear weaker readings from the back, push the hour.
Drop the front if it's outside the window.
From the first full window on, record the front's reading.

lines.text: The deque of candidate hours and the answer.

notes.java: An array with `head` and `tail` works as a deque: each index enters once, so `n` slots are enough.
notes.c: An array with `head` and `tail` works as a deque: each index enters once, so `n` slots are enough.

lines.text: A reading that's no higher than the new one, and older, can never be a peak again: remove it from the back. Then the new hour joins. The deque stays strictly decreasing.
The front is the oldest candidate; if it's now outside `i−k+1..i`, drop it. At most one index expires per step.
From the first full window on, the front is the highest reading in view.

complexity.md: **Time O(n):** every index enters and leaves the deque at most once. **Space O(k)** in the deque (it only holds indices inside the window); the C and Java versions allocate `n` slots for simplicity.

steps.text: Hour 3 (5): drop [-2, 1, 3] from the back (never a peak again while 5 is in view); push it. Peak of 1..3: 5.
Hour 6 (0): push it. The front (5) left the window: drop it. Peak of 4..6: 4.
Hour 7 (6): drop [0, 2, 4] from the back (never a peak again while 6 is in view); push it. Peak of 5..7: 6.

walk.title: A deque of indices whose readings decrease from front to back. The front is the current window's peak.

takeaways.md:
- **Sliding-window maximum = monotonic deque:** pop weaker items from the back, expired items from the front;
  the front is the answer.
- An item can be discarded as soon as a **newer, at-least-as-good** item arrives.
- Store indices, not values, so you can tell when the front has left the window.
